brewing.notes: A common starting point for herbal infusions: boiling water, about five minutes.

description:
A wild-gathered plant infusion from Shangri-La that is not true tea, found on dead larch and fir trunks above 4000 metres. It brews a red liquor.

Brew it as you would other herbal infusions. If the plant is new to you, check that it is safe for you first, especially when pregnant or on medication.
history: It is reported to have been used in Tibetan medicine for several centuries and, by local accounts, sent as tribute by the Mu chieftains in the Ming dynasty. It cannot be cultivated. Little more is reliably documented.
processing: Dried plant material, as with most herbal infusions.
harvest_season: Depends on the plant and the place.
appearance_liquor: Bright red, compared to red wine.
appearance_wet: The pieces open out in water like coral.
taste_profile: Described as slightly bitter with a sweet return and a shaded, woodland note.
vintage_note: Herbal infusions are not sold by vintage: buy recent stock and use it within a year or so.
